analysis.one_liner: A sweeping energy bill expanding federal support for oil, gas, coal and nuclear industries while extending low-income heating aid and electricity consumer protections.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared House committee in two days and was placed on the calendar of bills ready for floor action, but the record shows no floor vote before the 108th Congress ended without it becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This omnibus energy bill touches nearly every part of the energy economy. It fast-tracks approval of an Alaska natural gas pipeline, fills the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, exempts hydraulic fracturing from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection rules, gives fuel makers a safe harbor from lawsuits over the gasoline additive MTBE, repeals the 1935 Public Utility Holding Company Act, and extends federal nuclear liability indemnification to 2017. It also extends the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program at $3.4 billion a year, boosts weatherization funding, codifies the Energy Star program, creates appliance rebates, requires net metering, establishes enforceable electric reliability standards, and directs the FTC to write rules against 'slamming' and 'cramming' of electricity customers.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers get the fracking exemption, expedited Alaska pipeline approval, Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchases, and deepwater drilling research. Fuel makers get protection from MTBE contamination lawsuits plus federal cleanup and transition money. The nuclear industry gets extended federal backing of its liability, and coal gets clean coal funding. Low-income households get larger heating assistance and weatherization programs, and electricity customers get reliability standards, price transparency, and protections against unauthorized switches.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program at $3.4 billion for each of fiscal years 2004 through 2006 and raises weatherization funding to $325 million, $400 million, and $500 million in those years [S3].

Directs the Federal Trade Commission to write rules barring unauthorized switching of a customer's electric utility ('slamming') and unauthorized charges ('cramming'), and to protect the privacy of electricity consumers [S3].
Creates a statutory system of federally enforceable electric reliability standards through Electric Reliability Organizations subject to Federal Energy Regulatory Commission review [S2] [S3].

Requires each electric utility to offer net metering service on customer request and codifies the Energy Star efficiency labeling program, appliance rebates for consumers, and low-income community energy efficiency grants [S3].
Bans round-trip trades of wholesale electricity and directs FERC to create an electronic system giving the public timely access to market price information [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the research programs, Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchases, pipeline coordination, and MTBE cleanup. Communities whose groundwater has been contaminated by MTBE lose the ability to sue fuel makers, since the bill gives those fuels a safe harbor from litigation while shifting cleanup to federal funding. Costs of nuclear accidents above the industry's insurance layer would fall on the federal government through extended Price-Anderson indemnification.

drawbacks.text: The bill establishes a safe harbor for renewable fuels containing MTBE, a gasoline additive that has contaminated groundwater, and funds MTBE cleanup federally — protecting fuel makers from lawsuits while the public pays for the damage [S2] [S3].
It amends the Safe Drinking Water Act to exclude hydraulic fracturing fluids from the definition of underground injection, removing that drilling activity from federal regulation under the Act [S3].
It extends Price-Anderson nuclear liability indemnification to August 1, 2017, keeping the federal government on the hook for accident damages beyond industry coverage [S2] [S3].

It repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, removing long-standing consumer protections against utility holding company abuse, while relying on FERC market-transparency rules as the substitute [S2] [S3].
It instructs the President to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to full capacity, meaning large government purchases of oil that can tighten supply and push prices up for consumers [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The low-income energy aid, appliance rebates, reliability standards, and anti-slamming rules are genuine gains for ordinary people. But the bill's largest structural changes run the other way: a litigation shield for fuel makers over groundwater contamination, an exemption letting fracking escape Safe Drinking Water Act rules, extended federal liability backing for nuclear plants, repeal of the 1935 utility holding company law, and heavy federal research spending on oil, gas, coal, and nuclear programs. The industry-favoring provisions are broader and more durable than the consumer ones, and the bill bundles them all so opponents and supporters had to take the package as a whole.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, reported out of the Energy and Commerce Committee the next day, cleared six other committees by unanimous discharge two days later, and was placed on the House calendar of bills ready for floor action — but the record shows no floor vote, and the 108th Congress ended without it becoming law.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Barton of Texas introduced the Energy Policy Act of 2003 on April 7, 2003 [S1] [S2].
The House Energy and Commerce Committee reported the bill amended the next day, April 8, 2003, as H. Rept. 108-65 Part I [S3] [S6].

The bill was referred sequentially to five other committees, which were discharged on April 9, 2003, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 42 — the list of bills ready for floor consideration [S6] [S4].
The action history shows no further action after April 9, 2003, and the bill never became law during the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, fuel makers did not get their MTBE lawsuit shield, oil and gas producers did not get the fracking exemption, and the nuclear industry did not get its extended liability indemnification — but low-income households also lost the promised increases in heating aid and weatherization, and electricity customers lost the reliability standards and consumer protections. The main winners of the bill's failure were anyone who would have borne its costs: taxpayers and communities affected by contamination.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fuel makers and drillers lost their shields; aid never arrived

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote appears in the record, so there is no vote breakdown by party; the bill cleared committee with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill exempts hydraulic fracturing fluids from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection rules, fast-tracks Alaska pipeline approval with limits on federal conditions, fills the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and funds ultra-deepwater and unconventional drilling research. The liability and regulatory relief shifts contamination and siting costs onto the public.

A safe harbor shields fuels containing MTBE from litigation over groundwater contamination, while federal money funds cleanup and transition assistance to MTBE producers. Communities bearing contamination costs would pay instead.
Price-Anderson indemnification is extended to 2017, keeping the federal government liable for accident damages above industry coverage, alongside uranium mining research and nuclear R&D funding.

The bill authorizes a clean coal power initiative, university clean coal centers, coal gasification loan guarantees, and recovered-mineral mandates for federally funded cement. Federal support entrenches coal use while funding pollution-reducing technology.

Repeal of the 1935 Public Utility Holding Company Act frees holding companies from a major consumer-protection statute, but the bill also imposes enforceable reliability standards, market transparency rules, a round-trip trading ban, FTC slamming and cramming protections, and book-access requirements.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency industries
industries.note: Bioenergy, lighting, and renewable R&D authorizations, a renewable fuel mandate, net metering, appliance rebates, and Energy Star labeling expand markets for efficiency and renewable products that lower consumer bills.
